articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026. This action is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to target entities and individuals involved in activities that undermine U.S. sanctions against Iran.

Further details regarding the specific individuals or entities designated, and the nature of their activities, were not immediately available in the initial announcement. Such updates typically involve additions to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, imposing blocking sanctions on those listed.

This designation underscores the U.S. commitment to preventing Iran from accessing the international financial system and engaging in illicit activities, particularly those related to its nuclear program, support for terrorism, and human rights abuses.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. These actions aim to disrupt networks supporting the Iranian regime's illicit activities.

The specific individuals and entities targeted in these designations were not detailed in the initial announcement. OFAC frequently uses such designations to target those involved in Iran's proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, support for terrorism, and human rights violations.
These designations reinforce the U.S. government's strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran to alter its destabilizing behavior in the region and globally.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-Related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes Cuba Sanctions, and Publishes Cuba-Related Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a multi-faceted sanctions action on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new designations related to Cuba. This broad action underscores the U.S. commitment to combating illicit financial activities and supporting democratic principles.

The designations against cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations aim to disrupt global scam networks and the corporate infrastructure that enables them. OFAC also targeted a Malaysian individual accused of managing a network of Africa-based scammers targeting U.S. victims. Concurrently, OFAC published a Cuba-related Determination pursuant to Executive Order 14404, specifically identifying the 'Electronics, Manufacturing, Marine, and Technology Sectors of the Cuban Economy' as subject to sanctions.

Additionally, OFAC made changes to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List, including the re-designation of the vessel CARLOTA C as MARIA CRISTINA (CLBN) under both Venezuela and Cuba sanctions programs. These actions expand restrictions that can affect financial institutions and cross-border transactions, increasing compliance and reputational exposure to U.S. controls.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Updates Listings, Issues Alert, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of actions on November 4, 2026, including new Iran-related designations, updates to existing Iran-related listings, and the publication of an OFAC Alert concerning Iranian sanctions evasion. Concurrently, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a related Frequently Asked Question.

The Iran-related designations are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeting networks providing fraudulent vessel flags and maritime certifications to Iran's shadow fleet, as well as a Türkiye-based company supporting sanctioned Iranian airlines. The accompanying OFAC Alert warns the maritime industry about the substantial risk of designation or penalties for providing services to vessels using false flags to evade U.S. sanctions on Iran.

Furthermore, OFAC issued Venezuela-related General License 5AA, which authorizes, on or after December 18, 2026, transactions related to, financing for, and other dealings in the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 percent bond. This General License replaces and supersedes General License 5Z, whose authorization was scheduled to take effect on November 5.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / The Maritime Executive

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License FF-1
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of Iran General License FF-1 on October 29, 2026. This general license is titled 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.'

General License FF-1 provides a limited authorization for U.S. persons to engage in transactions that are ordinarily incident and necessary to wind down operations or existing contracts with the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance. The specific duration and scope of the wind-down period are detailed within the general license.
This action allows for an orderly cessation of business activities with the designated entity, minimizing unintended disruptions while maintaining the integrity of the Iran sanctions program.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Bank Data Insights

articles.region: North Korea / Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals Related to North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting individuals and entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to counter illicit activities and promote stability in both regions.

Under the North Korea sanctions program, OFAC added Russian and North Korean nationals linked to entities such as LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY ALIS, CHINYONG INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY COOPERATION COMPANY, and FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER. These designations target facilitators of DPRK IT worker fraud and those providing financial and material support to sanctioned North Korean entities.

For the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the designations include Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society (Zigama CSS), a Kigali-based financial institution. These actions are in response to Rwanda's destabilizing activities in Eastern DRC and support efforts to address widespread violence and atrocities in the region.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-headquartered cloud networking solutions provider, on October 27, 2026. The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and related services to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by designated entity JSC Concern Almaz Antey, even though MMZA itself was not directly listed on the SDN List until June 2022.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious, citing reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions and substantial harm to U.S. foreign policy objectives. Extreme Networks also entered into a parallel non-prosecution agreement with the Department of Justice, with a portion of the OFAC settlement deemed satisfied by payments under that agreement.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Corruption, Crime & Compliance

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Frequently Asked Questions on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced on October 26, 2026, the amendment of several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to blocking and rejecting transactions, and filing reports with OFAC. This update is part of an ongoing review to ensure guidance remains current.

The amended FAQs (numbers 10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53) clarify key aspects of sanctions compliance. These include guidance on which jurisdictions are subject to broad sanctions, how to block an account or funds transfer, the interest required on blocked funds, and when to reject rather than block a transaction.

The revisions also provide clearer explanations of reporting mechanics, including the requirement to file both blocked-property and rejected-transaction reports through the OFAC Reporting System (ORS) within ten business days, along with supporting documentation.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Sanctions Law Center

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of actions on October 21, 2026, including new Iran-related designations, removals from the Belarus and North Korea sanctions lists, and the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses.

Under the Iran sanctions program, OFAC added individuals and entities to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, including those linked to 'KARNAKIS AND KARNAKIS' and vessels associated with illicit Iranian activities. Concurrently, OFAC issued Iran General License GG and General License HH, authorizing wind-down activities and limited safety and environmental transactions involving certain blocked persons or vessels.

In a significant development, OFAC delisted Chinese national Lu Hezheng and two Chinese entities (Shanghai Moxing Cultural Media Co. Ltd. and Shanghai Hongman Cartoon and Animation Design Studio) from its North Korea sanctions program, and Belarusian national Andrei Alekseevich Rybakov from its Belarus sanctions program. Additionally, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131K, authorizing certain transactions for the negotiation and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Export Compliance Daily

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026, targeting entities involved in the theft of trade secrets from U.S. persons.

Five entities were designated, including Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Co Ltd (Zhisuan), Qiji Chuangtan Beijing Investment Management Co Ltd (MiraclePlus), Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase I Venture Capital Center Limited Partnership (Phase I), Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase II Venture Capital Center Limited Partnership (Phase II), and Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Zhiyuan Enterprise Management Center Limited Partnership (Zhiyuan Enterprise). These entities are linked to efforts to replicate U.S. super intelligence infrastructure technology.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, authorizing transactions pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, and PAIPA General License 2, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain entities blocked on October 19, 2026. These actions impose blocking sanctions and prohibit certain financial transactions with the designated entities.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Fined Over $1.5 Million by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations occurred between September 2018 and March 2022, when Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavard Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was deemed a blocked person due to its majority ownership by a designated entity, JSC Concern Almaz Antey, even though MMZA itself was not directly listed on the SDN List at the time of the transactions.
OFAC determined that the violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed. The company also entered into a parallel non-prosecution agreement with the Department of Justice.

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of 'Affiliates Rule' Until January 2027
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced an extension of the suspension of its 'Affiliates Rule' until January 10, 2027. This final rule, published in the Federal Register on November 9, 2026, postpones the implementation of expanded export controls that would cover companies owned by entities subject to certain U.S. trade restrictions.

The 'Affiliates Rule,' originally published on September 30, 2025, sought to extend existing end-user restrictions to companies owned 50% or more, directly or indirectly, by one or more entities appearing on certain U.S. restricted-party lists. The rule was initially suspended in November 2025 for one year as part of the U.S.-China Busan Agreement.

This latest extension provides an additional two months without introducing substantive changes to the underlying requirements, meaning exporters will not yet be required to apply the expanded ownership-based restrictions. The decision to further extend the suspension is likely influenced by broader political and geopolitical considerations.

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms, thereby alleviating compliance burdens on the firearms industry while continuing to protect national security.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors.

articles.headline: BIS Closes Export Controls Loophole for Foreign-Owned Semiconductor Fabs in China
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has closed a loophole that previously allowed a handful of foreign companies to export semiconductor manufacturing equipment and technology to China license-free.
This action means that these foreign-owned semiconductor fabrication facilities in China will now need to obtain licenses to export their technology, placing them on par with their competitors.

The move is aimed at strengthening U.S. export controls and preventing advanced technology from being used to further China's military modernization efforts, aligning with broader U.S. national security objectives.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
